# Sizing a power station for a fridge

You need to check three things: surge watts, running watts, and watt-hours.

**1. Surge watts (the spec that most often rules a unit out)**
- A compressor draws a brief startup spike. One guide puts it at about 1,200-2,400W for a household fridge ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). Another says about 1,200W is enough for typical models ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- Look for a surge rating of at least about 1,300W, and more for a large or older fridge. Check your fridge's manual if you can.
- Choose a pure sine wave inverter.

**2. Running watts**
A full-size fridge runs at roughly 100-250W, so almost any 1,000W-class station covers it.

**3. Watt-hours (how long it lasts)**
The compressor cycles on and off, so average use is far below the running watts.
- An ENERGY STAR 18 cu ft top-freezer averages about 41W, or roughly 1,000 Wh/day. With inverter losses and 20% headroom, plan on about **1,400 Wh per day** ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
- A large side-by-side with an ice maker can use about twice that.
- To get your own number, take the kWh/year on the EnergyGuide label, multiply by 1,000 and divide by 8,760. That gives average watts. You can also look up your model in the DOE's Refrigerator and Freezer Energy Rating Search Tool ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/how-to-size-a-portable-power-station-for-a-refrigerator-and-essential-devices/)).

## Quick guide
| Outage length | Capacity to look for |
|---|---|
| Part of a day | ~1,000 Wh. A 1,070 Wh unit is estimated at about 17 hours ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). |
| About 24 hours | ~1,400-2,000 Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800 Wh or more, or an expandable unit |

Keep the door shut during an outage. The USDA says food is unsafe after 4 hours above 40°F with the door closed ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).

## Options that fit
- **Roughly 1,000 Wh, for part of a day:** [BLUETTI AC180](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) has 1,152 Wh and 1,800W (2,700W peak). It was recently seen at $399-699. The [Jackery Explorer 1000 v2](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) was recently seen at $449-799.
- **About a full day:** [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l) has 2,048 Wh and 2,400W (3,600W surge). It's expandable up to 8 kWh and listed at $899, or $854.05 with a 5% code. The [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) has 2,010 Wh, 1,500W continuous and 3,000W peak, and was $699.99 after coupon on Anker's page.

Prices change often, so check them at checkout. For a typical fridge, I'd go with a ~2 kWh LiFePO4 unit if your budget allows. If you want multi-day backup or plan to add solar, the expandable AC200L is the better fit. If you also want to run other devices like a router or lights, add their watts to the total.
